Chronological is an adjective that describes things arranged in the order they happened in time, starting from the earliest and moving toward the most recent. It is all about time sequence — what came first, what came second, what came after that, and so on.

When something is described as chronological, it means time is the organizing principle. Nothing is shuffled around, skipped, or placed out of its natural time position. Everything sits exactly where it belongs on a timeline.

Think of time as a straight road. The road starts in the past and moves forward into the present, and then into the future. Chronological order means you travel down that road without turning back, jumping ahead, or taking detours. You go from Point A (the beginning) to Point B (the end) in a straight, uninterrupted line.

For example, if you were describing your day chronologically, you would say: "I woke up, then I brushed my teeth, then I had breakfast, then I went to school." That is chronological — each event is placed after the one that came before it in real time.

"Chronological" is used to describe things that can be arranged in time, such as events, steps, records, lists, stories, and accounts. Here are some natural examples:

A chronological list of events means the events are listed from the oldest to the newest.

A chronological account of history means the story of history is told starting from ancient times and moving forward toward modern times.

A chronological résumé is one where your jobs or education are listed starting from the earliest and going to the most recent — or sometimes most recent to earliest (see the note on reverse chronological order below).

A chronological narrative means a story told in the exact order things happened, without flashbacks or jumps in time.

Understanding what "chronological" is not makes it even clearer.

Non-chronological means the opposite — things are arranged in an order that does not follow the natural flow of time. Many novels, films, and stories are told in non-chronological order. For example, a film might begin by showing you the ending of the story, then jump back to show you how things started. That is deliberately non-chronological. A detective story might show you a crime first, then go back in time to reveal how it happened. Again, non-chronological.

So chronological order is the natural, time-based order, while non-chronological order breaks or rearranges that natural flow for some purpose.

You will often encounter the phrase "reverse chronological order," which simply means going from the most recent to the oldest — the exact opposite direction. Most social media feeds work this way: the newest post appears at the top, and the oldest post is at the bottom. Most modern résumés also use reverse chronological order, listing your most recent job first and your earliest job last. It is still organized by time; the direction is just flipped.

"Chronological" almost always appears alongside the word "order." The phrase "in chronological order" is extremely common. When someone says "please arrange these in chronological order," they are asking you to sort them from oldest to most recent.
Related Word Forms You Will Encounter

Knowing its close relatives will make the word fully yours:

Chronologically is the adverb form. It answers the question "how?" — for example, "The events are arranged chronologically." This means the same thing as "in chronological order."

Chronology is the noun form. It refers to the arrangement of events in time itself, or a document/account that presents events in time order. For example: "The book provides a chronology of World War II."

If you ever need to remember what "chronological" means, just ask yourself: "If I were filming life with a camera, pressing play from the very beginning and watching to the very end without fast-forwarding or rewinding — is that what this is?" If yes, it is chronological.

Chronological means arranged in the order of time, from earliest to latest. It describes any sequence — of events, steps, records, or stories — where the organizing principle is the actual passage of time. Its opposite is non-chronological (time order broken or rearranged), and its flipped version is reverse chronological (most recent first). The adverb is chronologically and the noun is chronology. The word is most commonly seen in the phrase "in chronological order."
